# Diagnosing Overheating and Bubbling in a Parked Vehicle

A vehicle that bubbles in the coolant overflow reservoir while parked is a classic symptom of a pressurized cooling system releasing vapor. This behavior indicates that the internal pressure within the engine block or cylinder head exceeds the boiling point of the coolant under static conditions. When you replaced the fluid four days ago and the system was fine immediately after, but it has returned to a low reservoir level with bubbling, the diagnosis shifts from a simple fluid exchange issue to a potential failure in maintaining system integrity or thermal equilibrium.

### The Physics of Coolant Expansion

To understand why this happens, you must look at the phase change of the working fluid. Water boils at 100Â°C (212Â°F) at sea level, but automotive coolant is a mixture designed to raise that boiling point significantly, often to 129Â°C or higher when mixed with ethylene glycol and pressurized. The radiator cap acts as a pressure valve, maintaining this elevated pressure inside the system.

When you see bubbles rising into the reservoir while the car is parked, you are witnessing vapor escaping. This occurs because the cap's spring pressure has likely failed, or the seal between the radiator neck and the cap is compromised. If the cap cannot hold the necessary pressure (typically 13.5 to 16.5 psi depending on the era of the vehicle), the coolant boils at a much lower temperature. As the engine heats up, even while sitting in a parking lot with no airflow from driving, the fluid expands into gas. This gas has nowhere to go but out through the overflow tube, filling your reservoir and preventing liquid from returning to the radiator when the engine cools.

### Evaluating the Radiator Cap

Your suspicion regarding the cap is technically sound. The cap is a pressure regulator, not just a lid. It contains a spring-loaded valve that opens at a specific pressure rating. Over time, the rubber gasket on the bottom of the cap can harden or crack, allowing pressure to bleed off before the boiling point is reached. Alternatively, the internal spring can weaken, causing the valve to open prematurely.

Replacing the coolant did not fix the underlying issue because you temporarily topped off a system that was already venting fluid faster than it could condense and return. The fact that the reservoir is very low now suggests one of two things: either there is an external leak that stopped briefly when the system was full (common with small cracks in hoses or gaskets), or the boiling-off rate has simply exceeded the fill rate during those four days.

### Investigating Internal Failures

While the cap is a high-probability suspect, it is not the only component to consider. If the bubbling persists immediately after replacing the cap and ensuring the system is sealed, you must investigate internal engine health. The most critical failure mode here is a blown head gasket. Combustion gases leaking into the coolant passages will force their way out through the overflow tube, creating bubbles that do not stop when the engine cools. This is distinct from simple vaporization caused by low pressure; combustion gas bubbles are usually more vigorous and continuous even after the engine has shut down for a significant period.

Another possibility is a failed water pump seal or a cracked cylinder head. If the head was warped due to previous overheating events, it may now be allowing gases to mix with the coolant. Checking for exhaust gases in the coolant using a block tester chemical kit is a definitive diagnostic step if external leaks and cap replacement do not resolve the bubbling.

### Implementation Strategy for Repair

If you are performing this repair yourself, start by verifying the pressure rating on your current cap against the specification on the radiator or owner's manual for your 2012 Chrysler 300. A mismatch in PSI ratings can lead to immediate boiling. Replace the cap if it is not within spec or shows signs of wear.

After replacing the cap, fill the system to the maximum level and run the engine to operating temperature with the radiator cap off (only when cool) to bleed air from the system. Air pockets trapped in the head or block can cause localized hot spots that lead to boiling regardless of the coolant's chemical properties. Once bled, reinstall the new cap and monitor the reservoir for at least two full drive cycles. If the fluid level drops significantly without bubbles, you have an external leak. If bubbles persist, you have confirmed an internal issue requiring further mechanical inspection.

Avoid using straight water as a temporary fix if the coolant mixture is off; it will lower the boiling point further and accelerate the problem. Use only the manufacturer-recommended 50/50 mix of ethylene glycol and distilled water to maintain the designed heat transfer characteristics and freezing protection.
